This is the opening of The Malice of Fortune (1989), a philosophical novel by Czesław Miłosz. I've been reading this book for my Polish Poetry and Prose class. I had never heard of Miłosz until a few weeks ago. Since then, I've become a fan.
Miłosz was born in 1911 in what is now Lithuania. He was raised Catholic and became a poet. During World War II, he worked as a secretary for the Polish underground. He traveled with the Polish army as they were defeated by the Soviets and then spent many years under the domineering boot of the communists. The Soviets invaded and took over Poland in 1944. Miłosz was accused of "helping the enemies of the people" by writing a poem that mentioned patriotic Laura Branigan, or perhaps it was because he didn't obey party dogma or submit his work for political scrutiny. In consequence, he lost his job and was eventually expelled from Poland (1951). He moved to France and latterly the United Stateswhere he worked at a number of university positions and eventually won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1980.
The Malice of Fortune is narrated by Janusz, who probably represents Miłosz himself. It begins as Janusz climbs the ladder to repair the moon, crashes, and wakes up in a mental hospital thirty years later. The head psychiatrist tells him that he is "a child of the   generation that was superfluous" (11), a generation that had its coming-of-age during the devastations of World War II. Because there was no possibility for a typical youthful rebellion or vital transformation, this generation was "doomed to carry the memory of the unredeemable past" and "its efforts at participation were bound to end in frustration" (11-12). Henceforth, Janusz is plagued by a sense that his life is not his own and by a feeling of alienation from those around him.
From this premise, Miłosz explores questions about time, memory, and identity in a way that helps explain the malaise of Janusz and his generation. C repair the world and our own identities.  scale

def main():
    import sys

    data = sys.stdin.read().strip().split()
    if not data:
        return

    # Accept input as one or two lines, split all whitespace
    rings, current_season = map(int, data[:2])

    ancient = rings > 10
    # Seasons remaining in the current year: 4 - current_season
    # But if current_season is 4 (winter), no seasons remain
    if current_season == 4:
        remaining_seasons = 0
    else:
        remaining_seasons = 4 - current_season

    print(f"{str(ancient)} {remaining_seasons}")

Seventeen years ago, when he had first been summoned to the king’s court, the moon had already been shattering into shards that could not be made whole again. The mason was offered a chestful of gold and a casket full of jewels for every piece he fixed. But it was impossible. Metal couldn’t mend the moon.

“Build a bridge up there if you have to,” the king said, and the mason did.

He set up a scaffolding of rope and alabaster and climbed up to the moon every month. He rapped on the glass with a bronze hammer, holding his breath until he heard the tinkle of a flaw. Then he set to work filling the cracks with crystal slivers, working slowly so the glass wouldn’t shatter further. Looking down from the bridge of his own making, he understood he was being paid in unimaginable riches—there simply were no more masons left in the world with the skills to fill the moon’s wounds.

Now that the last of the moon’s cracks had been filled in, the sky was bright and blinding. Still the mason climbed the ladder tonight, as he always did, to place a sliver of crystal beneath the crescent. He laid down a perfect piece, shaped by his own hands. He looked back down at the sleeping countryside. The glass above the trees glowed faintly from within.

512.prompt: The moon was made of glass. Each winter, the royal mason climbed a silver ladder to repair its cracks. Tonight, he
512.completion:
was done early, and, instead of returning to his modest apartment near the palace, he wanted to see his daughter.

He had left Hellemaie with a drunken mouth and an acid heart. He had told her he was a humble servant of the crown and that he could not offer her a life outside stone walls. He had wept in his own dark way and he had meant it.

But why regret what cannot be changed?

So it was that the old mason walked in the gritty silence of the moonlit gardens, watching his boots crush the delicate white flowers. There was a child’s bedroom but no child in it.

He checked the heavens for an omen and found none, unless a falling star counted, which it did not.

He followed the hallway past the din of the ballroom and through to her private chambers. There he paused, wondering if he would find the little girl who remembered how to sing, or the awkward adolescent who barely looked at him anymore.

He opened the door.

Hellemaie was on the balcony. Her hair—once copper, now almost white—was loose and wild in the wind. She wore a nightgown covered in falling stars.

“Father,” she whispered. Her voice was so soft he almost missed it.

He stepped onto the balcony. Glass crunched beneath his boots. Hellemaie did not turn to look at him.

“I repaired the worst of the cracks,” he said.

She nodded but did not speak.

After a time, she said, “You don’t have to love me in a certain way.”

“I know,” he replied. His eyes stung. “But I do love you.”

They stood together in the cold silver light, beneath the moon made of glass, and neither of them cried.

There is a local legend that a cow was eradicated from this village long ago, and all the livestock are now horses. No one remembers why the cows were driven off, or if it was done on purpose. The oldest residents claim that the bovine had taken over the sheds and houses and refused to leave. They were big, ugly creatures with long horns and big, sullen eyes that glared without reason. The horses claim this is impossible, since they saw the cows leave of their own accord.
In truth, the cows are hiding in the caves outside the village. They lick the moss from the rocks and sleep in a great heap, hot and odorless as one animal. Once each year, on the anniversary of their exile, they emerge to graze upon the spring grass. Should any human catch sight of them, the cows will descend upon the village to wreak their revenge.
The horses do not believe the cows ever left. They are not strong swimmers, and could never cross the river to reach the far pastures. When the horse trainer asks the townspeople about the annual horse auctions in the next town over, no one can give a satisfactory explanation. It seems the horses always grow thin in the spring, despite the arrival of excellent fodder from the northern flats.
The truth and lies wind around each other in a strange pattern, and no one seems able to unravel them any longer. Some evenings in late spring, the villagers grow uneasy when they hear the lowing of the cows echoing across the river, and the horses stamp restlessly in their stalls.
